newsitem.title: BRAZIL: South Korea's Kim sees investment boom in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's Kim sees investment boom in Brazil.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam told his Brazilian counterpart Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Wednesday that he foresaw a boom in Korean investment in Latin America's largest economy, officials said.

Kim predicted that his visit to Brazil, the first by a South Korean head of state, would result in $5 billion in investment over the next three years, almost double the $3.3 billion in Korean investment to date in all of Latin America.
He said Korean firms were particularly interested in telecommunications and mineral resources, Cardoso's spokesman, Sergio Amaral, told reporters.

On the penultimate leg of a Latin American tour, Kim signed accords with Cardoso on business visas, cooperation in tourism and regular political dialogue between Seoul and Brasilia. In addition to bilateral trade, the two leaders discussed multilateral issues such as the World Trade Organisation and United Nations reform.

Kim and Cardoso also touched on a simmering dispute over Brazilian car import rules that favour manufacturers with a local base and a recent move by Brasilia to impose punitive import quotas on Asian textile goods.
On the heels of a tour of the region by Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Kim has visited Chile, Guatemala and Argentina and was due to fly to Peru on Thursday.
Diplomats say the visits by Kim and Hashimoto reflected renewed faith in Latin American economies following widespread success in banishing the hyperinflation of the 1980s.

On Tuesday Brazil's soon-to-be privatized mining giant, Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, and South Korea's largest industrial conglomerate, Hyundai, signed a cooperation agreement to boost Brazilian exports of minerals, paper, timber and aluminum.

Another South Korean industrial power, Samsung, has announced plans to build a factory to manufacture television tubes in the Amazonian capital Manaus, where it already has a significant presence, churning out 300,000 television sets and 100,000 video recorders a year.
Cardoso told Kim Brazil was watching Korea's "rapid growth" with great interest and that he may visit the Asian country next year, Amaral said.
Any disagreements between the two governments over trade, such as the car and textile disputes, were billed as routine.

Brazil and Korea have long had friendly relations but trade and investment lagged during the 1980s while Korean businesses concentrated on Asia. The commercial relationship has taken off in recent years. Bilateral trade in 1995 amounted to some $2.9 billion, up from $700 million in 1990.
